section.title: The Mystery of the Gospel
section.sectionRationale: Having declared that Jew and Gentile are made one new humanity and one temple in Christ, Paul pauses to unfold the mystery behind it. He was entrusted with a stewardship of grace to make known a plan hidden for ages and now revealed: that through the gospel the Gentiles are fellow heirs, fellow members, and fellow partakers in Christ. This mystery is not private knowledge for insiders but God's public purpose, displayed even to the powers in the heavenly realms through the church.
section.thesis: The once-hidden, now-revealed mystery is that through the gospel the Gentiles share fully in Christ with Israel; to make this known God gave Paul, the least of the saints, a stewardship of grace, so that through the church the manifold wisdom of God might be displayed to the rulers and authorities, according to His eternal purpose accomplished in Christ, in whom we approach God with boldness.
section.frameNote: Three movements: Paul the prisoner and steward of the mystery revealed to him; the mystery itself, that the Gentiles are fellow heirs through the gospel; and the church as the theatre where God's manifold wisdom is displayed to the heavenly powers, giving believers bold access to God.

units.label: Paul, prisoner and steward of the mystery

verses.text: For this reason I, Paul, the prisoner of Christ Jesus for the sake of you Gentiles...
Surely you have heard about the {{oikonomia|stewardship}} of God's grace that was given to me for you,
that is, the mystery made known to me by revelation, as I have already written briefly.
In reading this, then, you will be able to understand my insight into the {{mysterion|mystery}} of Christ,

units.label: The mystery revealed: Gentiles fellow heirs

verses.text: which was not made known to men in other generations as it has now been revealed by the Spirit to God's holy apostles and prophets.
This mystery is that through the gospel the Gentiles are {{synkleronomos|fellow heirs}}, fellow members of the body, and fellow partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus.
I became a servant of this gospel by the gift of God's grace, given me through the working of His power.

units.label: The church displaying God's manifold wisdom

verses.text: Though I am less than the least of all the saints, this grace was given me: to preach to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ,
and to illuminate for everyone the stewardship of this mystery, which for ages past was kept hidden in God, who created all things.
His purpose was that now, through the church, the {{polupoikilos|manifold}} wisdom of God should be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly realms,
according to the eternal {{prothesis|purpose}} that He accomplished in Christ Jesus our Lord.
In Him and through faith in Him we may enter God's presence with {{parresia|boldness}} and confidence.
So I ask you not to be discouraged because of my sufferings for you, which are your glory.

oikonomia.gloss: Stewardship, the management of a household on behalf of its master, and by extension the administration of a plan. The word can describe both the office entrusted to a steward and the arrangement he administers. Paul received a stewardship of God's grace: not a possession to be proud of but a trust to be dispensed for the sake of others, faithfully distributing the riches of Christ to the Gentiles.

mysterion.gloss: A mystery, in the biblical sense not a puzzle or a secret guarded by the initiated, but a truth once hidden in God and now openly revealed. It is a plan too great for human discovery, made known only because God has disclosed it. Here the mystery of Christ is the uniting of Jew and Gentile in one body, a purpose kept in God for ages and now proclaimed to all through the gospel.

synkleronomos.gloss: Fellow heir, one who shares an inheritance jointly with others. Paul stacks three such syn compounds in verse 6, fellow heirs, fellow members of the body, and fellow partakers, to hammer home that the Gentiles do not stand on the margins as second-class dependents but share fully and equally with Israel in every blessing that belongs to those in Christ.

polupoikilos.gloss: Manifold, many-sided, richly varied, literally much-variegated, like an intricately woven or many-coloured fabric. The wisdom of God displayed in uniting Jew and Gentile in one body is not a single flat idea but a masterpiece of many colours, so dazzling that it is put on show even before the rulers and authorities in the heavenly realms, who learn God's wisdom by watching the church.

prothesis.gloss: Purpose, plan, that which is set forth beforehand. The uniting of the nations in Christ is no divine afterthought or emergency measure but the eternal prothesis, the settled purpose God formed before the ages and has now accomplished in Christ Jesus our Lord. The whole sweep of history moves within this fixed and gracious design.

parresia.gloss: Boldness, freedom of speech, the confident freedom to approach and to speak openly, without fear or shame. In Christ, and through faith in Him, believers may enter God's very presence with such boldness. The access opened in 2:18 is here felt as glad confidence: the reconciled sinner comes to God not cringing but freely, as a welcomed child of the household.

basic.context: Paul, a prisoner for the sake of the Gentiles, explains the plan behind everything he has said. God entrusted him with a stewardship of grace and revealed to him a mystery hidden for ages: that through the gospel the Gentiles now share fully with Israel as fellow heirs, fellow members, and fellow partakers in Christ. Paul, calling himself the least of all the saints, was given the task of preaching the unsearchable riches of Christ, so that through the church God's many-sided wisdom would be displayed even to the powers in the heavenly realms. All of this is God's eternal purpose, in whom we come to God with boldness.
basic.hermeneutics: The passage is a long digression that flows from the temple picture of chapter two and prepares for the prayer of 3:14. Paul breaks off in verse 1, I, Paul, the prisoner, and resumes the sentence in verse 14. In between he unfolds the mystery and his role in it. The key is to read mystery as Paul defines it in verse 6: not secret knowledge, but the open plan to unite Jew and Gentile in one body through the gospel.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul was given an oikonomia, a stewardship, of God's grace to dispense to the Gentiles. The mysterion, mystery, is the once-hidden, now-revealed plan of God. Its content is that the Gentiles are synkleronomos, fellow heirs, with Israel. Through the church the polupoikilos, manifold, many-coloured wisdom of God is displayed, according to His eternal prothesis, purpose, accomplished in Christ, in whom we approach God with parresia, boldness.
basic.typology: The stewards and prophets of the old covenant who guarded God's word find their fulfilment in the apostles and prophets to whom the full mystery is now revealed. The inheritance once bound up with the land and people of Israel opens out to all nations in Christ, the true heir, so that Gentiles become fellow heirs of the promise made to Abraham.
basic.christ: Christ is the content of the mystery, the mystery of Christ, and the one in whom Jew and Gentile are made fellow heirs. His unsearchable riches are what Paul preaches. He is the one in whom God's eternal purpose is accomplished, and through faith in Him we gain bold access to God. The whole plan of the ages centres and is realised in His person and work.
basic.god: God is the author of a plan formed before the ages and hidden in Himself, the Creator of all things who was working toward this all along. He is a God of manifold wisdom, whose glory is displayed even to the heavenly powers through the church. And He is the God who freely gives grace, to the Gentiles and to the least of the saints, and who now welcomes His people with boldness into His presence.
basic.crossReferences: Colossians 1 speaks of the mystery hidden for ages, now revealed, Christ in you the hope of glory. Romans 16 tells of the mystery kept secret for long ages, now made known to all nations. Galatians 3 makes the Gentiles heirs according to the promise. 1 Corinthians 2 speaks of God's secret wisdom revealed by the Spirit.
basic.oneStory: From the promise to Abraham that all nations would be blessed in his seed, God carried a plan that no one fully saw, guarded through Israel until the seed came. Now the veil is drawn back: in Christ the nations are fellow heirs, and the church becomes the display of God's wisdom before heaven and earth. The story of the ages is the unfolding of one eternal purpose, accomplished in Christ our Lord.

context.literary:
The most striking literary feature of these thirteen verses is that they begin a sentence and never finish it. Verse 1 opens with 'For this reason I, Paul, the prisoner of Christ Jesus for the sake of you Gentiles', and the grammar hangs there. Paul only returns to the thought in verse 14, 'For this reason I kneel before the Father', and a footnote in the BSB notes that the train of thought is continued there. The intervening verses are a parenthesis, though a better word is a deliberate long swerve, because Paul's mention of his own imprisonment prompts him to explain what his ministry is for.

Inside the swerve, the movement is clear. Verses 2 to 7 describe the revelation of the mystery and Paul's role as steward. Verses 8 to 10 turn to Paul's calling to preach it and God's purpose that the church display His wisdom to the powers. Verses 11 to 13 close with the eternal purpose fulfilled in Christ, the believer's access, and a plea not to be discouraged. Notice that the passage begins and ends with Paul's suffering, 'prisoner' in verse 1 and 'my sufferings for you' in verse 13. His chains frame the revelation of the mystery, and verse 13 says that these sufferings are the Gentiles' glory.

A second feature is the pile of compound words that begin with 'syn', meaning 'with'. In verse 6 the Gentiles are 'fellow heirs, fellow members, and fellow partakers', three compounds in a row that hammer one point home. A third feature is the contrast of hidden and revealed. Verse 5 says what was not made known to earlier generations, and verse 9 says it was kept hidden in God, set against the 'now' of verses 5 and 10. The passage then moves into the doxological prayer of 3:14 to 21, so that it forms a hinge between the teaching of chapters 1 to 3 and the prayers that close them.
context.historical:
Paul is writing from imprisonment, most likely in Rome, though the letter does not say where, and the Roman reading is the most widely held. A Roman prisoner could be chained to a guard, as in Acts 28:16 and 28:30, while receiving visitors. Paul calls himself 'the prisoner of Christ Jesus', not of Caesar. He sees his captivity as part of his service. The cause of his arrest was the Gentile question: the riot in Jerusalem began over the claim that he had taken a Gentile into the temple, Acts 21:28 to 29, and he told the crowd that the Lord had sent him to the Gentiles, Acts 22:21 to 22. When he writes 'for the sake of you Gentiles' he is stating a plain fact.

His claim to have received a revelation lines up with his own account elsewhere. In Galatians 1:15 to 16 he says God was pleased to reveal His Son in him so that he might preach Him among the Gentiles, and the Lord told Ananias that Paul was a chosen instrument to carry His name before the Gentiles, Acts 9:15.

Ephesus was a place where the language of mystery was familiar. Mystery religions were common in the Greek world, with secret rites reserved for initiates. Paul takes the word and turns it upside down. His mystery is not a secret kept for a select few but a plan to be announced to the whole world. The word also had a sense from Jewish apocalyptic writing, where God reveals hidden things about the future, as in Daniel 2:28 and 2:47, where God is the revealer of mysteries. Paul's usage is nearer to Daniel's than to the mystery cults.
context.canonical:
Paul's 'mystery' is a thread that runs through his letters. In Romans 16:25 to 27 he speaks of the mystery concealed for ages past but now revealed and made known through the writings of the prophets, in order to lead all nations to the obedience that comes from faith. In Colossians 1:26 to 27 the mystery that was hidden for ages and generations is now revealed, and its content is 'Christ in you, the hope of glory' among the Gentiles. In Romans 11:25 the mystery is the hardening in part of Israel until the full number of the Gentiles has come in. Ephesians 1:9 to 10 describes it as the mystery of God's will, to bring all things together in Christ. These are not different mysteries but facets of one plan.

The mystery is not entirely new, since Paul says in Romans 16:26 that it was made known through the prophets' writings. Isaiah 49:6 has the LORD say to His Servant that it is not enough merely to restore Israel; He will make Him a light for the nations, to bring salvation to the ends of the earth. Paul quotes this of his own mission in Acts 13:47. Genesis 12:3 already promised blessing to all the families of the earth. What was hidden was how it would happen: that Gentiles would come in as equal heirs, without becoming Jews, on the basis of Christ alone.

First Peter 1:10 to 12 adds a note that the prophets searched carefully into the grace that would come to the Gentiles and that angels long to look into these things, which corresponds to the audience of verse 10. First Corinthians 2:6 to 8 is a close companion: the hidden wisdom of God was not understood by the rulers of this age, who would not have crucified the Lord of glory if they had.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul has two aims here. The first is to show the Gentile readers that his imprisonment is not a reason for despair. He closes with 'I ask you not to be discouraged because of my sufferings for you, which are your glory', so the whole passage is a reply to an unspoken fear: if the apostle to the Gentiles is in chains, has the gospel failed? Paul says no. His chains are the price of their inclusion, and the plan they serve is older than the world.

The second aim is to make the readers see the church's dignity. Paul gives the church a role in a drama bigger than itself: through the church God's wisdom is displayed to rulers and authorities in the heavenly realms. A small and often despised congregation of former pagans is the stage on which cosmic powers see what God has done. That is meant to produce confidence and humility together. Paul is humbled by his calling, calling himself less than the least of the saints, and the church is exalted by its place in the plan.

He also wants his readers to be able to understand. 'In reading this, then, you will be able to understand my insight into the mystery of Christ' shows that Paul expected ordinary believers to follow and grasp the mystery. It is a revelation that is open to anyone who reads, not a secret held back for experts.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This is mostly description. Paul recounts what he received, how he was commissioned and what God's purpose is. The apostles and prophets who received the revelation in verse 5 are a particular group at the foundation, 2:20, and their reception of revelation is not a pattern for every believer to expect.

Two prescriptive elements stand out. The explicit one is the request in verse 13 not to be discouraged. The implicit one is the confident approach to God in verse 12. Believers are expected to come into God's presence with boldness, and the passage says this is possible 'in Him and through faith in Him'.

Paul's description of himself as a servant, a steward and the least of the saints is autobiography, not a template for everyone's calling. Yet it models something that applies to everyone: grace precedes service, and a servant of the gospel should be astonished at being used, as Paul says in 1 Corinthians 15:9 to 10. Paul's own role is unrepeatable, but the stewardship of the gospel has been passed to the whole church, which is why the manifold wisdom is shown 'through the church' and not through Paul alone.

debates.question: Was the mystery completely hidden before Christ, or only partly?

views.label: Hidden in the sense of not yet fulfilled or fully understood
views.case: Verse 5 says the mystery 'was not made known to men in other generations as it has now been revealed'. The word 'as' suggests a comparison of degree. Romans 16:26 says the mystery was made known through the prophets' writings, and Isaiah 49:6 promised light to the nations. The prophets saw the destination, but they did not see the way: Gentiles as equal members, in one body, with no entry through Israel's law. First Peter 1:10 to 12 says they searched to understand what the Spirit was pointing to.

views.label: Truly unknown before the revelation to the apostles and prophets
views.case: Others stress the force of 'kept hidden in God' in verse 9 and 'not made known' in verse 5. The Old Testament promised blessing to the nations, but the idea that Jews and Gentiles would be fellow members in one body without distinction was new. Paul says this was something revealed to the apostles and prophets by the Spirit, which suggests a real disclosure and not merely a clearer reading of old texts.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree that the content of the mystery, equal inclusion in one body, is now clear, and that it is revealed by the Spirit and not discovered by human insight. The question affects how we read the Old Testament: either as a text that already said this in outline or as one that left a gap that Christ filled.

debates.question: What does 'through faith in Him' in verse 12 mean?

views.label: Our faith directed toward Christ
views.case: The traditional reading takes the Greek pistis autou as an objective genitive: faith in Him. This fits the verse's emphasis on believers' access with boldness and confidence, and Romans 5:2 also says we have gained access by faith into grace. This reading matches Paul's usual stress on believers' trust.

views.label: Christ's own faithfulness
views.case: The BSB notes that the phrase can mean 'through His faithfulness'. On this reading the ground of our boldness is what Christ has done in His own faithful obedience, and our confidence rests on His faithfulness and not on the strength of our own trust. Advocates point to the same construction elsewhere in Paul and to the context, which is dense with what Christ has accomplished.

debates.bearing: The difference is smaller than it looks. Both readings agree that boldness before God depends on Christ, not on ourselves. The first stresses how we receive it, and the second what it rests on.

study.originalLanguages:
Begin with oikonomia in verse 2, which the BSB renders 'stewardship'. It comes from oikos, household, and nomos, law or management, and refers to the running of a household, usually by a trusted servant on behalf of the owner. Paul says God's grace was entrusted to him to be administered for the Gentiles. It is the same picture as in 1 Corinthians 4:1, where Paul calls himself a steward of the mysteries of God, and 1 Corinthians 9:17, where he says he is entrusted with a responsibility. A steward does not own what he handles, which fits the thrust of the passage.

Mysterion in verses 3, 4 and 9 does not mean a puzzle. In Paul's usage it is something once hidden and now disclosed, and verse 3 couples it with apokalypsis, revelation, to make the point. The word is defined in verse 6: 'that through the gospel the Gentiles are fellow heirs, fellow members of the body, and fellow partakers of the promise'. Each of the three terms begins with the same prefix syn, 'with': synkleronoma, syssoma and symmetocha. The middle one, syssoma, literally means 'joint-body'. The prefix shows that Paul wants the Gentiles to be understood as co-owners, not tenants.

In verse 8 Paul calls himself elachistoteros, 'less than the least'. It is an awkward comparative formed on a superlative, as if the grammar itself were bending under the weight of his humility. Compare 1 Corinthians 15:9, 'the least of the apostles', and 1 Timothy 1:15, 'of whom I am the worst'. Notice that the same man who says he is less than the least speaks without hesitation about his insight into the mystery, because his authority rests on a gift and not on himself.

Anexichniaston, 'unsearchable', in verse 8, describes riches that cannot be tracked out to their end. The related adjective appears in Romans 11:33 for God's ways. Paul is saying that the riches of Christ are not exhaustible even by the one who is commissioned to preach them.

The word polupoikilos, 'manifold', in verse 10 is made of 'many' and 'varied' and is used of something richly multicoloured, such as embroidery. The wisdom of God is not simple or monotone; it includes the bringing together of Jew and Gentile, the cross and the resurrection, and many other threads. The phrase prothesis ton aionon in verse 11 is literally 'the purpose of the ages', which the BSB renders 'eternal purpose': the plan belongs to the very structure of time.

Finally, verse 12 pairs parresia, 'boldness', which in other places means frank speech, with pepoithesis, 'confidence'. Prosagoge, 'access', recurs from 2:18. Verse 13 uses enkakein, 'to lose heart', a verb Paul uses of himself in 2 Corinthians 4:1 and 4:16, so he asks the readers to do what he himself has chosen to do.

typology.type: The steward of a household, Ephesians 3:2
typology.fulfillment: Old Testament history has stewards in the sense of trusted servants who administer another's house, such as Joseph in Potiphar's house and then in Pharaoh's, Genesis 39:4 and 41:40. Paul is a steward of God's household in the new age. The escalation is that what he administers is not food but the grace of God, and not for one nation but for the Gentiles. The pattern is imperfect because Paul is only a servant, and the true Steward over God's house is the Son, Hebrews 3:5 to 6.

typology.type: The Servant who is a light to the nations, Ephesians 3:8
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah 49:6 says the Servant is to be a light to the nations as well as to restore Israel, and Paul takes up this calling for his own ministry in Acts 13:47. In Acts 26:17 to 18 Jesus tells him he is being sent to the Gentiles to open their eyes so that they turn from darkness to light. The escalation is that the Servant's own mission is carried on through His apostle and through His church. The type falls short in that Paul is a light only by reflection; the true light is Christ, and Paul only carries it.

typology.type: Prophets searching for the grace to come, Ephesians 3:5
typology.fulfillment: First Peter 1:10 to 12 says the prophets searched and investigated carefully the grace to come, and that the Spirit of Christ in them pointed to Christ's sufferings and the glories to follow. Their words held more than they knew, and Paul says it is now revealed to the apostles and prophets. The correspondence is between the Old Testament pointing and the New Testament unveiling. The pattern is limited because the prophets served a message they did not live to see, while the apostles can say that it has now happened.

typology.type: Wisdom made known to powers, Ephesians 3:10
typology.fulfillment: The Old Testament is full of scenes where God's rule is acknowledged before heavenly beings, such as Job 1:6 and Psalm 82. The cross is the greatest display of wisdom, which Colossians 2:15 describes as disarming the powers and authorities and making a public spectacle of them. In Ephesians the church is where the powers watch the wisdom unfold. The escalation is that the display is not given by fire or a vision but by a community of redeemed sinners. The type falls short in that the powers only observe; they are not themselves redeemed, Hebrews 2:16.

study.christ:
The word 'Christ' occurs at the very centre of this passage and also at its edges: 'the prisoner of Christ Jesus' in verse 1, 'the mystery of Christ' in verse 4, 'the unsearchable riches of Christ' in verse 8, and 'Christ Jesus our Lord' in verse 11. The mystery is not an abstract plan; it has a name. Colossians 1:27 states it directly: 'Christ in you, the hope of glory.' What was hidden in God is a person.

The mystery's content in verse 6 is that the Gentiles are fellow heirs 'in Christ Jesus'. The inheritance is not detached from Him. Israel's hope was always an inheritance given to a seed, and Paul says in Galatians 3:16 that the seed was Christ, which explains why those joined to Him are heirs together. The whole structure of Gentile inclusion depends on being in the Heir, since there is no other way in.

Verse 11 says that God's eternal purpose was 'accomplished in Christ Jesus our Lord'. The verb is about doing or making, and it points to the cross and resurrection as the place where the plan was carried out. Colossians 2:15 says that by the cross God disarmed the powers and made a public spectacle of them, and 1 Corinthians 2:8 says the rulers of this age crucified the Lord of glory without understanding. Ephesians 3:10 therefore adds that the same powers are now taught the wisdom of God through the church. The cross they brought about in ignorance is the means of their instruction.

Verse 12 describes the believer's access. Because Christ has brought us near, 2:13, we come into God's presence with boldness and confidence. Hebrews 4:16 and 10:19 draw the same conclusion in the language of the throne of grace and the Most Holy Place. The new freedom of access is not our achievement. Christ is the way, John 14:6, and the passage shows what that means for people who were once outsiders.

A word of caution. Paul does not say that the Old Testament is full of hidden references to a Gentile church. The passage speaks of a mystery newly revealed, and the Old Testament promises are best read as pointing toward something whose shape was not clear until Christ. It is better to see promise and fulfilment than to find the church in every verse.
study.god:
This passage shows a God who plans. The purpose of verse 11 is 'eternal', literally a purpose of the ages, and verse 9 says the mystery was kept hidden 'in God, who created all things'. The same God who made everything had a plan for it from the beginning. History is not a series of improvisations; it is the unfolding of a purpose, which Ephesians 1:9 to 10 already stated as bringing all things together in Christ. Paul would have us worship the God who is never taken by surprise.

He is also a God who reveals. The mystery is made known 'by revelation' and 'by the Spirit', verses 3 and 5. Human wisdom did not find it, and 1 Corinthians 2:7 to 10 says the same: God has revealed it by the Spirit, who searches even the deep things of God. The God of the Bible is not silent; He takes the initiative to speak, and He does so in order to be known.

God's wisdom is called 'manifold', richly varied. It is wise enough to use the cross, which the rulers of this age did not understand, and to build one family out of the two groups that history had set against each other. Wisdom here is not abstract; it is shown in what God does with a church.

God is also gracious in how He chooses His servants. Paul describes himself as the least and writes of the gift of grace given 'through the working of His power', verse 7. The one who persecuted the church is trusted with the gospel, as 1 Timothy 1:15 to 16 says, so that Christ might display His perfect patience. God's strength shows best in weak instruments, and He does not hold their past against them.

The last picture is of a God who invites us in. In verse 12 we may enter His presence with boldness and confidence. That fits Paul's wider teaching that the Father welcomes those who come through Christ. And the God who plans, reveals and shows wisdom is also the God who is close and approachable. Worship in response is both awed, because the riches are unsearchable, and bold, because the door is open.

One tension should be kept: the plan is eternal and sovereign, yet Paul's suffering is real and costly, and the passage does not explain it away. He says his sufferings are for the readers' glory, which is a way of saying that God's sovereign purposes run through human pain, as 2 Corinthians 4:17 also says, without making the pain pleasant.

crossReferences.note: The closest parallel. Paul rejoices in suffering for the church, calls himself its servant by God's commission, and names the mystery hidden for ages and now revealed as 'Christ in you, the hope of glory' among the Gentiles. It shows that Ephesians 3 and Colossians 1 are two statements of one apostolic message.

The mystery was concealed for ages past but is now made known through the prophets' writings, so that all nations come to the obedience that comes from faith. This answers the question of how hidden the mystery was: it was in the Scriptures, but unseen until now.

Paul speaks of God's hidden wisdom, destined for our glory before time began, which the rulers of this age did not grasp, or they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. It explains why the powers need to be taught in Ephesians 3:10: they acted in ignorance.

The LORD tells His Servant that restoring Israel is too small a task, and that He will be a light for the nations, bringing salvation to the ends of the earth. This is the Old Testament source of the Gentile mission that Paul says he was given, and Paul uses it of himself in Acts 13:47.

God set Paul apart from the womb and was pleased to reveal His Son in him so that he might preach Him among the Gentiles. It shows that Ephesians 3:3 is no after-thought: Paul's calling and his message about the Gentiles came together.

Paul calls himself the least of the apostles because he persecuted the church, and says that it is by the grace of God that he is what he is. It stands behind 'less than the least' in Ephesians 3:8 and gives the reason for his humility.

The prophets searched carefully into the grace that was to come, and it was revealed to them that they were serving others. Even angels long to look into these things. It parallels the two audiences of Ephesians 3, prophets who looked ahead and heavenly beings who look on.

Paul gives another mystery: a hardening in part has come upon Israel until the full number of the Gentiles has come in. It shows the Jewish side of the same plan, and warns Gentile believers against conceit, which Ephesians 3 prevents by pointing to grace and not merit.

After Daniel interprets the dream, Nebuchadnezzar calls God the Revealer of Mysteries. This is the Old Testament root of the Pauline use of mystery: something known to God that He chooses to disclose. It shows that the idea of divine revelation of hidden things is a biblical one and not drawn from pagan mystery cults.

God disarmed the powers and authorities and made a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them by the cross. Ephesians 3:10 describes their instruction through the church, and Colossians 2:15 describes their defeat at the cross. The two passages are two sides of the same victory.

The mystery of God's will is a plan for the fullness of time to bring all things in heaven and on earth together in Christ. This is the larger frame for the particular mystery of chapter 3: the union of Jew and Gentile is a first instalment of the gathering of everything under Christ.

Believers are invited to approach the throne of grace with confidence to receive mercy. It matches Ephesians 3:12, and the pairing shows that the boldness described there is not presumption but an invitation grounded in the work of the high priest.

study.oneStory:
The story begins with a God who made all things, a point Paul makes in verse 9, and with human beings who were to rule the earth under Him. The fall brings the first great question: how will God keep His purpose for the world and the human race now that sin has entered? The answer is not stated at once. It is promised in a seed who will crush the serpent, Genesis 3:15, and in a blessing for all the families of the earth, Genesis 12:3. Paul's mystery is the answer to that long question, and he says that the answer was prepared before creation, 'kept hidden in God, who created all things'.

For centuries the answer appeared in shadow. Israel was called and set apart. The prophets spoke of a light for the nations, Isaiah 49:6, and of foreigners who would join themselves to the LORD, Isaiah 56:6 to 7. Daniel saw the kingdom of God filling the earth. But nobody, including the prophets, could see how Gentiles would be brought in fully equal, and 1 Peter 1:10 to 12 says the prophets searched for it.

The cross and resurrection are the turning point, and Paul's own conversion, a persecutor made an apostle, is a small copy of it. The mystery is revealed to the apostles and prophets by the Spirit, and Paul is sent to preach it. The book of Acts reads as the first chapters of this mission, as the gospel moves from Jerusalem to Rome.

The passage also anticipates the future. The church is displaying God's wisdom to the heavenly powers now, and that display will be complete when God brings all things together in Christ, Ephesians 1:10. At the end of the story the nations walk by the light of the city of God, Revelation 21:24, and the mystery that was hidden for ages is the open secret of the new creation. The least of the saints sits with the Gentiles at the feast, in the presence of the God who planned it before the world began.

quiz.q: What does Paul mean by the mystery in this passage?

options.text: A plan once hidden in God and now openly revealed: that Gentiles are fellow heirs with Israel in Christ.
options.note: Paul defines it in verse 6; it is disclosed and preached to all, not secret lore.

options.text: A truth that remains secret and known only to a select few.
options.note: Paul says it is illuminated for everyone and preached openly to the Gentiles.

options.text: A puzzle that human wisdom eventually worked out on its own.
options.note: It was made known by revelation and the Spirit, not by human discovery.

options.text: A teaching that has nothing to do with the Gentiles.
options.note: The mystery is precisely that the Gentiles are fellow heirs through the gospel.

quiz.q: How does Paul describe the Gentiles' standing in verse 6?

options.text: Fellow heirs, fellow members of the body, and fellow partakers of the promise in Christ.
options.note: Three syn compounds stress full and equal sharing with Israel.

options.text: Guests who may observe Israel's blessings from a distance.
options.note: They share fully as fellow heirs, not as onlookers.

options.text: Members on probation until they adopt the law.
options.note: They are already fellow heirs through the gospel, not on probation.

options.text: Permanently excluded from the promise.
options.note: The whole point is their inclusion as fellow partakers of the promise.

quiz.q: What role does the church play according to verse 10?

options.text: Through the church God's manifold wisdom is displayed to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly realms.
options.note: The church is the theatre of God's many-coloured wisdom before the heavenly powers.

options.text: The church exists mainly to keep social order on earth.
options.note: Its role here is far larger: to display God's wisdom even to heavenly powers.

options.text: The church hides God's wisdom from the world.
options.note: The wisdom is made known, put on display, not hidden.

options.text: The church has no part in God's cosmic purpose.
options.note: Paul places the church at the centre of God's eternal purpose.

quiz.q: How does Paul describe himself in relation to this ministry?

options.text: Less than the least of all the saints, given grace to preach the unsearchable riches of Christ.
options.note: Paul marvels that such grace and stewardship were given to one so unworthy.

options.text: The greatest of the apostles, deserving of the task.
options.note: He calls himself the least of the saints; the stewardship is all of grace.

options.text: A reluctant messenger who resents the calling.
options.note: He counts it grace and calls his sufferings the Gentiles' glory.

options.text: An independent teacher with his own private message.
options.note: He received the mystery by revelation and shares it with the apostles and prophets.

quiz.q: What is the eternal purpose Paul speaks of in verse 11?

options.text: God's settled plan, formed before the ages and accomplished in Christ Jesus our Lord.
options.note: The uniting of the nations in Christ is no afterthought but God's eternal purpose.

options.text: A backup plan God devised after His first plan failed.
options.note: It is an eternal purpose, not an emergency measure.

options.text: A purpose still waiting to begin at some future date.
options.note: Paul says it is already accomplished in Christ Jesus our Lord.

options.text: A purpose that bypasses Christ altogether.
options.note: The purpose is accomplished precisely in Christ Jesus our Lord.

quiz.q: What confidence do believers have in Christ according to verse 12?

options.text: They may enter God's presence with boldness and confidence through faith in Him.
options.note: The access of 2:18 is felt here as glad, bold freedom to approach God.

options.text: They may approach God only through appointed human mediators.
options.note: Access is through Christ and faith in Him, not through other mediators.

options.text: They must approach God cringing and uncertain of welcome.
options.note: Paul says boldness and confidence, the freedom of a welcomed child.

options.text: They have no real access to God at all.
options.note: In Him we may enter God's presence with boldness and confidence.

questions: Paul calls the gospel a mystery once hidden and now revealed. How does it change your reading of Scripture to see the whole Old Testament quietly carrying a plan now unveiled in Christ?
The Gentiles are fellow heirs, fellow members, and fellow partakers with Israel. Where are you tempted to see any believer as second-class, and how does this equal standing in Christ correct that?
God displays His wisdom to the heavenly powers through the church. How does it lift your view of your own local congregation to know it is part of that cosmic display?

Paul calls himself the least of the saints yet entrusted with unsearchable riches. How does the idea of stewardship, a trust to dispense rather than a possession to keep, reshape how you use the grace you have received?
In Christ you may come to God with boldness and confidence. What would change in your prayers this week if you truly approached God as a welcomed child rather than an anxious outsider?

translationNotes.note: The verse ends with an ellipsis in the BSB because Paul breaks off his sentence, the prisoner of Christ Jesus for the sake of you Gentiles, and resumes the thought in 3:14; the ellipsis marks the interruption.

The Greek stacks three compounds beginning with syn, together: fellow heirs, fellow members of the body, and fellow partakers, underscoring that the Gentiles share fully and equally with Israel in Christ.
Some manuscripts read the fellowship of the mystery rather than the stewardship of this mystery; the sense in either case is the administration and disclosure of God's once-hidden plan.

meta.notes: BSB text for Ephesians 3:1-13 reproduced as supplied, including the ellipsis at the end of verse 1.
